description: Make your data come alive. Learn to build fully interactive, web-ready charts with hover tooltips, zooming, animations, and sliders using Plotly.

slides.title: Interactive Visualizations
slides.content:
# The Problem with PNGs 🖼️

Matplotlib and Seaborn generate static images (PNGs). They are great for printing on paper or embedding in a PDF.

But on the web, users expect interactivity. They want to hover over a data point to see its exact value, zoom into a dense cluster, or toggle lines on and off in the legend.

**Plotly** is an open-source graphing library built entirely on top of JavaScript (React/D3.js). When you write Python code, Plotly translates it into interactive HTML/JS that renders directly in the browser!

slides.title: Plotly Express
slides.content:
# The High-Level API: Plotly Express 🚀

Plotly has a low-level API (Graph Objects) and a high-level API called **Plotly Express (`px`)**.

Plotly Express is the recommended starting point. It operates almost exactly like Seaborn, accepting Pandas DataFrames directly.

```bash
pip install plotly pandas
```

```python_not
import plotly.express as px

# Plotly has built-in datasets too!
df = px.data.iris()

# Create an interactive scatter plot
fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length")

# Opens the interactive chart in your web browser!
fig.show()
```

slides.title: Adding Dimensions
slides.content:
# Color, Size, and Hover 🎨

Just like Seaborn, we can add dimensions. But with Plotly, we can also customize the interactive tooltips!

```python_not
fig = px.scatter(
    df, 
    x="sepal_width", 
    y="sepal_length", 
    color="species",      # Like Seaborn's 'hue'
    size="petal_length",  # The bubble size!
    hover_data=['petal_width'] # Extra data to show on hover!
)
fig.show()
```

When the browser opens, try hovering over a bubble. You will see all the data points listed cleanly.

slides.title: A World of Charts
slides.content:
# Basic Charts 📊

Plotly Express makes standard charts a breeze.

```python_not
gap = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")

# Bar Chart
fig_bar = px.bar(gap, x="continent", y="pop", color="continent")

# Line Chart
fig_line = px.line(gap, x="country", y="lifeExp")

# Pie Chart
fig_pie = px.pie(gap, values="pop", names="continent", title="Population")
```

slides.title: Plotly Basics Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of the Plotly ecosystem.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the primary difference between a chart generated by Seaborn and a chart generated by Plotly?
quizOptions: Plotly charts are static PNG images, while Seaborn charts are interactive.
Seaborn generates static images (perfect for PDFs/paper), while Plotly generates interactive HTML/JavaScript objects (perfect for web dashboards).
Plotly is built on top of Matplotlib.

slides.title: Advanced Express Charts
slides.content:
# Beyond the Basics 🗺️

Plotly Express handles highly complex chart types out of the box.

**Choropleth Maps** (Coloring geographic regions):
```python_not
fig = px.choropleth(gap, locations="iso_alpha", 
                    color="lifeExp", 
                    hover_name="country",
                    color_continuous_scale=px.colors.sequential.Plasma)
```

**Sunburst Charts** (Hierarchical data):
```python_not
fig = px.sunburst(gap, path=['continent', 'country'], values='pop')
```

slides.title: Animations
slides.content:
# Motion in Data 🎬

One of Plotly Express's most powerful features is one-line animations.

By specifying an `animation_frame` (usually a Time or Year column), Plotly automatically builds a slider and a Play/Pause button!

```python_not
df = px.data.gapminder()

fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", 
    animation_frame="year", # This triggers the magic!
    animation_group="country",
    size="pop", color="continent", hover_name="country",
    log_x=True, size_max=55, 
    range_x=[100,100000], range_y=[25,90]
)
fig.show()
```

slides.title: Graph Objects API
slides.content:
# The Low-Level API: `go` ⚙️

Plotly Express (`px`) returns a `Figure` object. 

Sometimes, `px` doesn't support the exact complex layout you need. When that happens, you must use the underlying **Graph Objects (`go`)** API. It is more verbose, but provides infinite customization.

```python_not
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Create an empty Figure
fig = go.Figure()

# Add "Traces" (layers of data) manually
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 1, 2], mode='lines', name='Line 1'))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[2, 4, 6], mode='markers', name='Line 2'))

# Update the overall layout
fig.update_layout(title='Manual Graph Objects', xaxis_title='Time')
fig.show()
```

slides.title: API Quiz
slides.content: Ensure you know when to use which tool.
slides.quizQuestion: In the Plotly ecosystem, when should you use the `plotly.graph_objects` (`go`) API instead of `plotly.express` (`px`)?
quizOptions: When you need to export the chart as a PDF.
When Plotly Express does not support the highly specific, custom, or complex chart layout you need to build.

slides.title: Subplots
slides.content:
# Multiple Charts: `make_subplots` 🪟

To create a grid of separate charts (like Matplotlib's `plt.subplots`), you use the `make_subplots` utility alongside Graph Objects.

```python_not
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Create a 1x2 grid
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("Plot 1", "Plot 2"))

# Add traces to specific rows/cols
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=[4, 2, 1]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(y=[2, 1, 3]), row=1, col=2)

fig.show()
```

slides.title: Secondary Y-Axis
slides.content:
# Twin Axes ♊

What if you want to plot Temperature (0-100) and Revenue (0-1,000,000) on the exact same chart? The temperature line would be crushed to the bottom.

You need a Secondary Y-Axis on the right side of the chart.

```python_not
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Must explicitly enable the secondary y-axis
fig = make_subplots(specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}]])

# Add the primary trace (Left Axis)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=[20, 25, 22], name="Temperature"), secondary_y=False)

# Add the secondary trace (Right Axis)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(y=[4000, 5000, 3000], name="Revenue", opacity=0.5), secondary_y=True)

fig.show()
```

slides.title: Custom Controls
slides.content:
# Buttons and Sliders 🎛️

Using the `go.Figure.update_layout` method, you can add native HTML UI elements directly to the chart, allowing the user to filter data without writing a full web app.

```python_not
import plotly.graph_objects as go
fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Scatter(y=[1, 3, 2])])

# Add a dropdown menu
fig.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            buttons=list([
                dict(args=["type", "scatter"], label="Line Chart", method="restyle"),
                dict(args=["type", "bar"], label="Bar Chart", method="restyle")
            ]),
            direction="down", showactive=True
        )
    ]
)
fig.show()
```

slides.quizQuestion: If you need to plot two completely different datasets on the same chart (e.g., one dataset ranges from 0-10, the other ranges from 1,000-10,000), what feature should you use to ensure both are readable?

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Interactive Master! 🎉

You've learned how to build production-ready, interactive web charts.

## Key Takeaways

- ✅ **Web First:** Plotly generates interactive HTML/JS, not static images.
- ✅ **Plotly Express (`px`):** The high-level API. Start here! It supports animations, maps, and integrates flawlessly with Pandas.
- ✅ **Graph Objects (`go`):** The low-level API. Use it when you need ultimate control over traces, axes, and layouts.
- ✅ **Subplots & Secondary Axes:** Use `make_subplots` to build complex grid layouts and twin axes.
- ✅ **Interactivity:** Every chart features built-in hover tooltips, zooming, and panning. You can also add custom sliders and dropdowns.

Next, we'll look at alternative interactive libraries like Altair.
